confirmed: Read the complete markdown conversion (including references and Appendix A) and checked the cited numerical passages against PDF text. The source is the 22-page arXiv:2607.18564v2 preprint stamped 22 Jul 2026, in an ACM template; the recorded title and authors match the document (PDF p. 1; PDF page count).

The user study is a within-subjects HALO-versus-baseline comparison; condition order and task pairing were counterbalanced, but random allocation is not stated (PDF p. 8, Sections 6 and 6.1.2). Retain assignment.randomized='not_stated' and criterion_1='unclear'; other/none remain provisional classifications pending allocation clarification, rather than asserting either randomized or known non-random allocation.

The appendix's explicit random selections concern generation-prompt templates, not people, interface conditions, or condition order (PDF p. 22, Figure 13). No randomized people study is established by the full text.

Ten medicinal chemists from nine labs were recruited and ten completed the user study; the same people experienced both conditions. Ten analyzed people per condition and ten total are supported, while n_randomized remains null; the study is below the 50-person threshold (PDF p. 8, Section 6.1.2; p. 9, Section 6.1.4; p. 11, Section 7.4; p. 21, Table 4).
The main-study participants are P3-P12, postdoctoral and senior researchers with 8-15 years of experience. No exclusions are reported (PDF p. 9, Section 6.1.4; p. 21, Table 4; p. 11, Section 7.4).

Each task lasted 30 minutes, with a five-minute break, 10-minute instruction, and five-minute practice; the sessions were remote via Zoom. Each participant submitted seven molecules per condition, which are outputs rather than additional participants (PDF p. 8, Section 6.1.2; p. 10, Section 6.2.4).

Both arms contain the generative molecule model and an LLM interface; the baseline omits MolCluster, MolStrategy, and MolSynthesis. Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct fine-tuned on C-MuMOInstruct and Gemini 3 Flash are the model names printed in the appendix (PDF p. 8, Section 6; pp. 16-18, Sections A.1, A.5, and A.6).

Quality values are exactly Baseline 2.25 ± 0.48 and HALO 3.16 ± 0.37, with p = 0.0039**; Table 1 labels these mean ± standard deviation, and the text names the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (PDF p. 9, Table 1; p. 10, Section 6.2.4).

The row labeled Diversity reports exactly Baseline 58.27% ± 11.01% and HALO 46.07% ± 7.68%, with p = 0.0039**. These are average within-participant Tanimoto similarities, so lower values mean more varied submitted molecules; the text names the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (PDF p. 9, Table 1; p. 10, Section 6.2.4 and Equation 1).

The one-line finding reproduces the correct means, similarity percentages, p-values, and within-participant interpretation. It should not be interpreted as evidence of reduced similarity across different people (PDF p. 9, Table 1; p. 10, Section 6.2.4).

The quality endpoint is a model-based property-improvement score, without wet-lab validation. Section 6.2.4 attributes evaluation to ADMET-AI, while the implementation appendix also specifies Therapeutic Data Commons oracles and RDKit descriptors; these implementation details should not be flattened into an independently verified common scorer for every property (PDF p. 10, Section 6.2.4; p. 11, Section 7.4; p. 16, Section A.1).

Core exclusion and criterion_2='not_met' are supported by the ten-person sample; criterion_3='met' is supported by scored submitted molecules. This is not a synthesis, so the default synthesis counts and pooled-effect fields need no estimates (PDF pp. 8-11, Section 6 and Section 7.4; pp. 16-17, Section A.2).
summary: The counterbalanced HALO user study analyzed ten chemists, with random assignment not stated, so no randomized people study is confirmed and the sample is below the core threshold. The headline statistics match Table 1, but omitted studies, incomplete coding, appendix metadata, molecular-similarity coding, and an unsupported participant-level quality-analysis claim require correction.
